newsitem.title: UK: Britain's coronation stone to go to Edinburgh.
newsitem.headline: Britain's coronation stone to go to Edinburgh.

text.p: The coronation stone used by British monarchs since the Middle Ages is to be moved to Edinburgh Castle later this month, 700 years after the English king Edward 1 seized it from the Scots and took it to London.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth announced on Monday that the Stone of Scone would be transferred on November 30, feast day of St Andrew, Scotland's Patron Saint.

In what was seen by some opposition politicians as a sop to nationalist sentiment in Scotland, the government said in July that it planned to move the 400-pound (180-kilo) sandstone slab, also known as the Stone of Destiny, back north of the border.

Over the past four months, Scots have launched competing claims to house the stone. Suggestions of where it should go on display have ranged from the New Arlington Bar in Glasgow to Scone Palace near the village from which it originated.

But Forsyth decided on the imposing fortress that dominates the Scottish capital and in which are kept Scotland's crown jewels and other treasures such as the circle of gold worn by Robert the Bruce at the 14th century Battle of Bannockburn.
"The living symbols of Monarchy - the Stone of Destiny and the Honours of Scotland - will...be displayed side by side," he said.
The stone, which traditionally lies under the throne when British kings and queens are crowned, will be taken back to London's Westminster Abbey temporarily for future coronations.
The stone, used for the coronation of Scottish kings before 1296, was once a potent symbol for Scottish nationalists -- a group of them stole it in 1950 but it was retrieved after a few months.
Scotland lost its independence in 1707 when it was merged into a single British state with England and Wales.

The pro-independence Scottish National Party, and other opposition parties which plan to set up a separate tax-raising parliament for Scotland, say the decision to move the stone is a meaningless gesture to Scottish sentiment.

The ruling Conservatives, which oppose any devolution of powers to Scotland, have been steadily losing support north of the border for years. But the decision on the stone has done little to improve its position there.
The latest Scottish opinion poll showed Conservative support at only 13 percent, well behind both Labour and the Scottish Nationalists.
